recorded: Late 1953 or January 1954; Salle Adyar, Paris (Commons attribution)
question: How can a refrain return clearly when the voices keep overlapping?
intro: Couperin lets notes overlap across changing basses, softening the edges between chords. Marcelle Meyer plays this harpsichord rondeau on piano; follow the returning refrain through the interlocking parts.

sections.label: Refrain · overlapping voices
sections.mNote: low-register refrain establishes the overlapping texture

sections.label: First two couplets and refrain returns

cues.title: Chords arriving in layers
cues.text: The parts do not strike every chord together. Held notes overlap the moving bass, and short upper figures keep renewing the sound. Follow one inner voice rather than treating the piano as a succession of solid chords.
cues.evidence: Couperin’s score shows independent durations and tied notes in the low-register refrain. The analysis reports continuous attacks across the opening; this describes the texture, not a precisely aligned suspension. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP128589-WIMA.0099-Couperin_6eOrdre_Les_Baricades.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Church and royal chamber
cues.text: Couperin combines Parisian church duties with royal employment. He becomes an organist of Louis XIV’s chapel in 1693; his four harpsichord books appear between 1713 and 1730.
cues.evidence: Opéra Royal’s Couperin biography documents the chapel appointment and four harpsichord books: https://www.operaroyal-versailles.fr/genre-event/couperin/

cues.title: A refrain among episodes
cues.text: This is a rondeau: the opening refrain returns between contrasting couplets. The recurring overlap of the voices makes those returns less like a restart than a recovery of a familiar pattern.
cues.evidence: The score explicitly marks Rondeau and three couplets. The report has boundaries near 0:18, 0:30, 0:44 and 0:52, but does not establish every return; this note explains the whole design rather than announcing a particular bar.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A deliberately puzzling title
cues.text: The piece belongs to the sixth ordre in Couperin’s second harpsichord book, published in 1717. The title names no securely identified scene: a story about the “mysterious barricades” is not needed to follow the musical refrain.
cues.evidence: The score identifies the sixth ordre and 1717 book. The Opéra Royal biography discusses the unresolved titles; the existing Couperin biography likewise distinguishes interpretations from an established programme. https://www.operaroyal-versailles.fr/genre-event/couperin/

cues.title: The longer final excursion
cues.text: In the extended last couplet, listen for the bass moving beneath a pattern that remains recognisable. The episode has more room to continue its sequences before the short refrain brings the piece back to its starting texture.
cues.evidence: The score’s third couplet is substantially longer than the earlier episodes. Its broad placement after about 0:52 fits the report’s 0:52–1:10 changes and the stronger level windows at 0:55, 1:05 and 1:10; individual sequences are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A piano, not a harpsichord
cues.text: Marcelle Meyer is the pianist in this transfer, not a harpsichordist. The source identifies a Les Discophiles Français issue and a Salle Adyar session in late 1953 or January 1954; the 2023 date belongs to the upload.
cues.evidence: Commons distinguishes its Author/session information from the 23 September 2023 upload. Classical Pianists independently lists the Couperin programme under 1953/1954 and DF 86. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:François_Couperin_-_Les_barricades_mysterieuses_(Marcelle_Meyer,_1954).flac

transitions.title: A new episode keeps the overlap
transitions.how: The first couplet continues the refrain’s staggered attacks and low register. Changing bass notes and upper-voice details distinguish the episode without a new tempo or instrument. The later return restores the familiar refrain; the map groups the first two couplets with their intervening returns rather than inventing a boundary for every phrase.
transitions.evidence: The written first couplet follows the repeated refrain. The 0:18 measured boundary supports the approximate passage division; no bar alignment has been made.

transitions.title: The same mechanism lasts longer
transitions.how: After another refrain, the third couplet extends the chain of moving bass notes and overlapping upper parts. Sequential continuation carries the familiar rhythmic mechanism farther before the return. Its greater length, rather than a change of instrumental colour, makes this the principal excursion.
transitions.evidence: The score marks a third, longer couplet. The 0:52 boundary and subsequent changes at 0:56, 1:06 and 1:10 support a broad final-episode span, not a timed chord analysis.

transitions.title: The short refrain closes the circle
transitions.how: Couperin directs the player back to the rondeau instead of adding a separate closing tune. The familiar B♭-major texture is recovered and the final ending allows the voices to settle together. In this transfer, the returning passage withdraws after the preceding rise in level.
transitions.evidence: The score’s final Rondeau direction supplies the return. Relative level drops from −3.2 dB at 1:10 to −11.6 dB at 1:15 and −23.9 dB at 1:25; the 1:16 map point is approximate, not the identified first note of the refrain.

fields.note: The nominated file contains the individual character piece, not the complete sixth ordre. The work was published in the 1717 second book. composer.epithet: A Parisian organist whose harpsichord pieces turn ornament, delayed resolution and the timing of a released key into structural events.
facts: Nephew of Louis Couperin; succeeded his father Charles at Saint-Gervais
Organist of Saint-Gervais from 1685; royal chapel organist from 1693; royal chamber harpsichordist from 1717
Four books of harpsichord pieces, 27 ordres; organ masses, chamber music, motets and Leçons de Ténèbres
composer.background:
François Couperin belonged to a family whose connection with the organ of Saint-Gervais in Paris lasted for generations. His father Charles died in 1679, when François was ten; Michel-Richard de Lalande temporarily held the post intended for the boy. Couperin took it up in 1685. His uncle Louis, who had died before François was born, had already established a distinctive harpsichord language of broken chords, dance rhythms and unmeasured preludes. The younger Couperin inherited a profession and a repertory. His own published harpsichord music would increasingly substitute named character pieces for a predictable succession of dances.

In 1693 he won one of the four organist positions at Louis XIV’s royal chapel. Serving by quarter, he combined court employment with his Parisian responsibilities. He taught members of the royal family and took part in chamber performances; in 1717 he became a royal chamber harpsichordist. These overlapping appointments help explain his range: a musician who supplied an organ verset for a service might also teach the fingering of an ornament or play a concert with violin and viol.
